extracted.intended_audience: readers and scholars of political theory, American institutions, and nineteenth-century social analysis
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and synthesizing the claims and evaluative principles Alexis de Tocqueville uses to assess race relations, the condition of Native Americans and African-descended peoples, and the social effects of European colonization in North America.

rubrics_metrics.name: Author's principal aim
rubrics_metrics.description: “to portray democracy has been my principal aim.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tocqueville states that portraying democracy is the central purpose of his work; other collateral questions are postponed and taken up only as the proper termination of the study.

rubrics_metrics.name: Race classification and hierarchy
rubrics_metrics.description: “Three races, naturally distinct... Almost insurmountable barriers had been raised between them by education and by law... they are mixed, and each race fulfils its destiny apart.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text treats the white/European, the negro, and the Indian as distinct social types with legally and culturally enforced separations; Tocqueville uses this tripartite classification as a framework for evaluating social dynamics in the United States.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effects of oppression on the negro
rubrics_metrics.description: Oppression has deprived descendants of Africans of almost all the privileges of humanity; the negro 'remains half way between the two communities... finding not a spot in the universe to call by the name of country.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tocqueville describes multiple consequences of slavery: loss of language, religion, customs, family structure, internalized servility, degraded understanding, lifelong status beginning before birth (purchased in the womb), and the paradox that emancipation can leave freed persons unprepared for independence. Use these consequences as criteria when assessing the social condition produced by slavery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effects of oppression and displacement on the Indian
rubrics_metrics.description: Europeans 'dispersed the Indian tribes and driven them into the deserts, condemned them to a wandering life full of inexpressible sufferings' and their 'moral and physical condition... continually grew worse.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text emphasizes forced migration, loss of attachment to country, breakdown of family and tradition, increasing misery, and eventual disappearance as criteria for judging the impact of European expansion on Native populations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impact of European settlement on subsistence resources
rubrics_metrics.description: From the moment when a European settlement is formed... the beasts of chase take the alarm... 'the buffalo is constantly receding'... famine compels them to recede.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tocqueville treats environmental/resource effects (game displacement, declining fur availability) as a proximate cause forcing Indigenous peoples to abandon lands; these ecological and economic disruptions are key metrics for understanding displacement and decline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prerequisite for civilization: fixation and agriculture
rubrics_metrics.description: “In order to succeed in civilizing a people, it is first necessary to fix it; which cannot be done without inducing it to cultivate the soil; the Indians ought in the first place to have been accustomed to agriculture.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tocqueville asserts that permanent settlement and agriculture are necessary preconditions for the social processes labeled 'civilization' because civilization requires transmission of habits across generations; absence of fixation and aversion to tillage count as barriers to assimilation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two survival alternatives for Indian nations: war or civilization
rubrics_metrics.description: “The savages of North America had only two ways of escaping destruction; war or civilization—They are no longer able to make war... they will never conform to civilization.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tocqueville frames the future of Native nations as dependent on either mounting effective military resistance or successfully assimilating; he uses the availability and likelihood of these options to predict extinction or survival.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methods and mechanics of land acquisition from Indians
rubrics_metrics.description: Government envoys assemble Indians, offer goods (firearms, woollen garments, kegs of brandy, glass necklaces) and use insinuation and intimidation so that 'half convinced, and half compelled, they go to inhabit new deserts' — resulting in large cessions for trivial payments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The narrative treats the use of gifts, alcohol, manufactured goods, manipulation of immediate wants, and implicit threats as systematic tactics for acquiring Native lands; incidence, scale, and fairness of such transactions are criteria for assessing settler-state policy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultural obstacles to assimilation: labor, honor, and values
rubrics_metrics.description: Indians 'consider labor not merely as an evil, but as a disgrace' and valorize war and hunting as the only pursuits worthy of a man; industry is compared 'to the ox which traces the furrow.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tocqueville highlights values and status structures (shame attached to agricultural labor; honor attached to war exploits) as cultural metrics that impede adoption of European modes of life and thus serve as explanatory criteria for resistance to 'civilization.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of mixed-blood populations in assimilation
rubrics_metrics.description: The growth of European habits has been remarkably accelerated among these Indians by the mixed race... the half-blood forms the natural link between civilization and barbarism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tocqueville identifies mixed-race individuals as mediators who transmit European habits and institutions; the presence and influence of mixed descent populations (and examples like the Cherokees adopting written language, government, and newspapers) are treated as indicators of the degree of assimilation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indicators of assimilation and institutional adoption
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples such as the Cherokees creating 'a written language; established a permanent form of government; ... set up a newspaper' are cited as signs of adoption of European-style civilization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adoption of written language, formal government structures, press/newspapers, and agriculture are presented as concrete markers used to evaluate whether a tribe has taken up 'civilized' institutions.
